title: New Born
wpTitle: Born With Teeth reviews round-up – starring Ncuti Gatwa & Edward Bluemel in the West End [Updated]

ratings.excerpt: Former Doctor Who and Sex Education star Ncuti Gatwa has done it all over again … Will we see two better star turns this year? I doubt it. As Winston Churchill might almost have said, Ncuti Gatwa, playing hell-raiser playwright Christopher Marlowe and Edward Bluemel, as a bashful William Shakespeare, have nothing to offer us but ‘blood, sweat, tears and... laughter’ in Liz Duffy Adams’ fascinating drama Born With Teeth … Such is the intensity of their performances under a phalanx of lights on all sides, the two actors are literally dripping in sweat. … But even more impressive than his physique is Gatwa’s playfully feline disposition. Yes, his character is prepared to betray friends and lovers to secure his fortune. … ... Daniel Evans’s steamy production fizzes with rare theatrical chemist

Seductively clever work from Ncuti Gatwa … Liz Duffy Adams blends intrigue and shifty eroticism with in-jokes and a discourse on creativity in this playful examination of Kit Marlowe and Shakespeare’s relationship … Phwoar! The chance to see a jacked and shirtless Ncuti Gatwa snogging his snake-hipped, chisel-cheekboned former Sex Education co-star Edward Bluemel is undoubtedly part of the appeal of Liz Duffy Adams’s seductively clever two-hander. … Her play blends intrigue and shifty eroticism with in-jokes and a discourse on creativity. … Duffy uses the now-familiar trope of blending period and modern idioms but does so with aplomb. … The script is also full of nods to both writers’ work, which could be smug and irritating but works here. … Bluemel is an engaging Will, wary and diffident

Fascinating encounters between Marlowe and Shakespeare … ... Liz Duffy Adams’ firecracker of a play Born With Teeth … ... Daniel Evans’ steamy, sensationally acted RSC production … At its heart, this is a piece about narrative control, about art under censorship, and about the way writers can reach down through centuries to give us the truth of their times. It’s fascinating, fun and flawed. … It’s a tantalising piece — for better and for worse. It’s greatly entertaining, peppered with literary gags and impish anachronisms, and delivered with immense flourish. What holds it back is a reluctance to dive deeper into the huge themes it raises and give its characters more time to explore loaded issues … But it does gradually grow in nuance and gravity, and it’s dazzlingly performed. … ... the e

Edward Bleumel and Ncuti Gatwa thrill in intoxicating Shakespeare drama Born With Teeth … Elizabethan bromance with Ncuti Gatwa and Edward Bleumel in Born With Teeth … From the moment young, callow Will takes the stage to give us a little background intro and the frontcloth explodes in images of screaming tortured men, it is clear that director Daniel Evans isn’t aiming for a night of subtle rumination. … Blazing with the energy of a feral genius, Gatwa’s Kit is a cousin to Caravaggio, a swaggering, bisexual smartass who would rather drink, fight and flirt than write. … The language is fierce, funny and conjures the era without attempting to ape it. … f you want a more serious examination of Christopher Marlowe’s complex personality, see Peter Whelan’s The School of Night or read Anthony B

Ncuti Gatwa’s Marlowe gets steamy with a bisexual Shakespeare … Born With Teeth dares to dramatise an imagined affair between the playwrights – diverting but ultimately toothless … 90 minutes of entertaining hokum... What a steamy affair she conjures, potently assisted by Ncuti Gatwa as the homosexual Marlowe and Edward Bluemel as an ardent, if wavering bisexual Bard. … It’s tragi-comical-farcical-ludicrous. What keeps you watching is the lusty bravura of Gatwa... with Bluemel (a rising star from Amazon Prime’s My Lady Jane) neatly evoking Shakespeare’s growing confidence and gnawing doubts. … Whether you’re resistant or receptive to the main premise, there’s delight to be had in seeing a friskily rivalrous rapport form between the famous duo, even if we’re given little tangible sense of t

Fun but trashy two-hander in which William Shakespeare and Kit Marlowe have a sexy time … For much of its running time Daniel Evans’s RSC production comes across like a particularly insane workplace comedy … There are laughs, but it’s not in fact a comedy: there is a core of po-facedness that becomes more apparent as the play wears on. Shakespeare’s star waxes; Marlowe’s starts to wane, as his relentless outrageousness starts to annoy people in power. … Born with Teeth is pretty trashy. I rolled my eyes at the whole sexual tension thing … Evans directs with considerable force  and zero period fluff … Ultimately what Born with Teeth suffers from the most is asking us to imagine a sex and paranoia crazed Elizabethan society while not actually showing it to us. … But I can’t help but feel she

Ncuti Gatwa simmers in Elizabethan battle of the playwrights … Gatwa’s Christopher Marlowe and Edward Bluemel’s William Shakespeare flirt, fight and write in Liz Duffy Adams’ sizzling new chamber play … Enjoying the historical license her character grants her, Duffy Adams whips the competitors into a frenzy and releases them at each other’s throats, letting them flirt, threaten, fight - and very occasionally write. But the bold imagination Kit calls for in reframing history is restrained by Daniel Evans’ staging. … Bursts of violent action are reserved for mid-act screens, though tension is diffused as Will steps out to address the audience, undermining the intensity of the locked-door environment. … ... this is Gatwa’s show. His boisterous Kit sweats in Zoë Thomas-Webb’s leather two-piece

Ncuti Gatwa stars in Shakespeare fan fiction … The Dr Who actor gets sweaty as Christopher Marlowe, opposite Edward Bluemel as the Bard, in this sprightly two-hander … Liz Duffy Adams’s sprightly two-hander about the relationship between Christopher Marlowe and a young William Shakespeare reimagines them as hot, horny lads with very 21st-century minds. … ... the play — premiered in the US in 2022 and now retooled for the West End — has the air of an ingenious revue sketch stretched to outsize proportions. … You wait in vain for this Marlowe to acquire some nuance when he flirts with Edward Bluemel’s ingenuous Will … At its heart, though, it hovers at the level of conscientiously researched fan fiction.

Ncuti Gatwa and Edward Bluemel are playwrights dancing with death … It’s an odd confection, at once challenging and comic, slightly circuitous and oddly revealing. … The dialogue is snappy, and often very funny. “We’re the same age, … Not in stage years, … But there’s also a lot of under-explained allusion to historical figures and their circles; background colour that makes sense if you know, but not a lot if you don’t. … But it is the acting that holds you. Gatwa is electricfying as Marlowe, all flashing wit and sexy swagger … As Shakespeare, Bluemel is surprisingly endearing...It’s a performance full of grace and charm.

Born With Teeth is too cerebral - but Ncuti Gatwa saves the day … The Doctor Who star carries this swashbuckling drama about William Shakespeare and his underappreciated rival Christopher Marlowe … Born With Teeth is, without doubt, the sort of drama that would sit more comfortably in Stratford upon Avon than the West End and is in London for one reason only: the star wattage of Doctor Who himself, Ncuti Gatwa … I’m delighted to report that Gatwa is in his swashbuckling element here, infinitely more compelling than he was in The Importance of Being Earnest … Bluemel gives an understated performance of someone growing in confidence, growing into themselves, whereas Gatwa’s Marlowe is a flame that burns with explosive brightness and is then extinguished.

Ncuti Gatwa peacocks and flirts his way through this radical play … Liz Duffy Adams’ Tudor fan fiction stars Gatwa and Edward Bluemel as rivals Christopher Marlowe and William Shakespeare – it’s just a shame it didn’t dig deeper … ... this sharp, saucy period drama by US playwright Liz Duffy Adams. And with Ncuti Gatwa in the role, you can well believe it. … ... there’s more than a hint of romantic tension to this exercise in Tudor fan fiction. … Here, Gatwa revels in his role to an almost distracting degree... But what he doesn’t do is bare his soul, or show the inner torment of a man so obsessed with power and political intrigue that he’ll sacrifice everything else, even his happiness. … Born With Teeth is built on abundant research into both Shakespeare and his fascinating rival Marlowe

Ncuti Gatwa and Edward Bluemel dazzle in this slight, stylish two-hander … Part historical fantasia, part parlour game of literary in-jokes... it makes a smooth-running star vehicle for dazzling turns from Ncuti Gatwa as Christopher Marlowe and Edward Bluemel as William Shakespeare … Duffy Adams’ touch is featherlight, and the play is undemanding fun with just a whiff of pretension … But while that celerity guards against the piece becoming ponderous, it comes at the price of dramatic and emotional heft. Nothing that happens here ever feels as if it matters much. … Themes of artistic immortality, authorship and the nature of inspiration float through the writing, alongside discussion of religion... I’d rather have done my taxes than watch this pointless play with Ncuti Gatwa … Born with Teeth is the kind of night at the theatre I like least: it’s too good to dismiss, too unengaging for me not to long for it to end … It did sound like the kind of what-if? bio-drama I’d make every effort to swerve at the Edinburgh Fringe, though. What if Charlie Chaplin were stuck in lift with Marcel Marceau in 1950s Paris? … It’s really not terrible. Duffy Adams can certainly craft a line.
